propositions.text: The appeal concerns the proper approach to interpreting the scope of a release and whether special interpretive rules apply.
propositions.quote: This appeal is about the proper approach to interpreting the scope of a release, whether there is any special interpretive rule that applies specifically to releases, and if not, how the general principles of contractual interpretation this Court set out in Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., 2014 SCC 53, [2014] 2 S.C.R. 633, apply to the release at issue here.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns how to interpret a release and if special rules apply, referencing Sattva principles.

propositions.text: Mrs. Bailey struck Mr. Temple; Mr. Temple sued Mrs. Bailey; Mrs. Bailey sued the City; they settled and Mrs. Bailey released the City.
propositions.quote: The respondent Mary Bailey struck David Temple, an employee of the appellant City of Corner Brook, with her husband’s car. Mr. Temple sued Mrs. Bailey. In a separate action, Mrs. Bailey sued the City. Mrs. Bailey and the City settled, and Mrs. Bailey released the City from liability relating to the accident and discontinued her action.

propositions.text: Mrs. Bailey later brought a third party claim against the City; the City says the release bars it; Mrs. Bailey says it does not.
propositions.quote: Years later, Mrs. Bailey brought a third party claim against the City for contribution or indemnity, in the action brought against her by Mr. Temple. The City says the release bars Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim. Mrs. Bailey says it does not.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the factual background and the dispute over whether the release bars Mrs. Bailey's third party claim.

propositions.text: No special interpretive principle applies to releases; the Blackmore Rule is outdated and replaced by Sattva principles.
propositions.quote: There is no special interpretive principle that applies to releases. The decisions below refer to the rule from the House of Lords decision in London and South Western Railway Co. v. Blackmore (1870)... The Blackmore Rule has outlived its usefulness and should no longer be referred to.

propositions.text: Judicial tendency to interpret releases narrowly is due to releases themselves, not a special rule.
propositions.quote: Any judicial tendency to interpret releases narrowly is not a function of any special rule, but rather a function of releases themselves.

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds no special rule applies to releases; the Blackmore Rule is outdated and replaced by Sattva.

propositions.text: The application judge interpreted the release broadly per Sattva and made no reviewable error.
propositions.quote: In the instant case, the application judge interpreted the release broadly to include Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim in accordance with Sattva, and his reasons should have been reviewed on a palpable and overriding error standard.

propositions.text: The appeal should be allowed and the application judge's order reinstated.
propositions.quote: As the application judge made no reviewable error in his interpretation of the release, I would allow the appeal and reinstate his order.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds no error in the application judge's broad interpretation and would allow the appeal, reinstating his order.

propositions.text: On March 3, 2009, Mrs. Bailey struck Mr. Temple while driving her husband's car; Mr. Temple was working for the City.
propositions.quote: On March 3, 2009, Mrs. Bailey struck Mr. Temple while driving a car owned by her husband. Mr. Temple was an employee of the City of Corner Brook, and was performing road work at the time.

propositions.text: The Baileys sued the City for property damage and Mrs. Bailey's injuries in the Bailey Action.
propositions.quote: The Baileys commenced an action against the City for property damage to the car and physical injury suffered by Mrs. Bailey (“Bailey Action”).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the accident facts and the Baileys' lawsuit against the City.

propositions.text: Mr. Temple sued Mrs. Bailey for his injuries in the Temple Action; Mrs. Bailey was served on March 24, 2011 and informed her insurer.
propositions.quote: Meanwhile, Mr. Temple commenced a separate action against Mrs. Bailey seeking compensation for the injuries he sustained in the accident (“Temple Action”). Mrs. Bailey was served with the statement of claim in the Temple Action on March 24, 2011. Once served, Mrs. Bailey brought the statement of claim to her insurance representative.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes Mr. Temple's lawsuit against Mrs. Bailey and her response.

propositions.text: The Baileys and City negotiated settlement; Baileys offered $10,000; City countered $7,500 with release and discontinuance conditions; Baileys accepted.
propositions.quote: Subsequently, the Baileys and the City entered into settlement discussions via their counsel... The Baileys signed the release on August 26, 2011.

propositions.text: The release broadly discharged the City from all claims relating to the March 3, 2009 accident, including claims raised or that could have been raised in the Bailey Action.
propositions.quote: the [Baileys]... hereby release and forever discharge the [City]... from all actions... arising out of or relating to the accident which occurred on or about March 3, 2009, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing from all claims raised or which could have been raised in the [Bailey Action]

paragraphs.summary: The Court details the settlement negotiations and the broad release terms signed by the Baileys.

propositions.text: On March 16, 2016, Mrs. Bailey commenced a third party claim against the City in the Temple Action for contribution or indemnity.
propositions.quote: Later, on March 16, 2016, Mrs. Bailey commenced a third party claim against the City in the Temple Action, claiming contribution or indemnity from the City in the event she is found liable to Mr. Temple in his claim against her.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Mrs. Bailey's third party claim against the City in 2016.

propositions.text: The City applied for summary trial to bar the third party claim based on the release; Mrs. Bailey opposed, arguing the claim was not contemplated by the release.
propositions.quote: The City brought a summary trial application pursuant to Rule 17A... The City’s position was that the release barred the third party claim. Mrs. Bailey’s position was that it did not, because the third party claim was not specifically contemplated by the City and the Baileys when they signed the release.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the summary trial application and the parties' opposing positions on the release's scope.

propositions.text: Justice Murphy found the release barred Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim and stayed it, applying the Blackmore Rule to interpret the release.
propositions.quote: Justice George L. Murphy concluded that the release barred Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim against the City and stayed the claim. He began by acknowledging... the Blackmore Rule.

propositions.text: Interpreting a release requires ascertaining parties' intention objectively, looking at words and context.
propositions.quote: He explained that in interpreting a release, the goal is to ascertain the intention of the parties. The court must first look to the words of the release. It may also look to the context in which the release was signed to interpret those words. The review must be carried out from an objective perspective.

paragraphs.summary: The application judge found the release barred the claim, applying the Blackmore Rule and an objective interpretation of words and context.

propositions.text: The release's words cover the third party claim, but the Blackmore Rule requires considering parties' contemplation at signing.
propositions.quote: The application judge concluded that based on the words of the release alone, it covers Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim. However, this did not end his analysis, because the Blackmore Rule required him to consider what was in the contemplation of the parties at the time the release was signed and the specific context in which it was signed.

propositions.text: Mrs. Bailey was served with the Temple Action before signing the release and knew facts underlying the third party claim.
propositions.quote: The application judge noted that Mrs. Bailey had already been served with the Temple Action when she signed the release, and that the statement of claim in the Bailey Action demonstrated that she was aware of the facts underlying the third party claim when she signed the release.

propositions.text: Reviewing counsel correspondence, the judge concluded parties contemplated all claims relating to the accident.
propositions.quote: He then reviewed the correspondence between counsel leading up to the release, and concluded that the parties contemplated any and all types of claims relating to the accident.

paragraphs.summary: The application judge found the release covered the claim and parties contemplated all accident-related claims at signing.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal unanimously allowed the appeal, overturning the application judge's decision.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal unanimously allowed the appeal.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule is subsumed into general contractual interpretation principles from Sattva and Ledcor.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal concluded that the Blackmore Rule has, over time, been subsumed into the principles of contractual interpretation affirmed by this Court in Sattva and Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., 2016 SCC 37, [2016] 2 S.C.R. 23.

propositions.text: Whether applying Blackmore or not, the result in this case is the same.
propositions.quote: Whether one approaches the appeal based on the Blackmore Rule or not, the result in this case would be the same.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding Blackmore is subsumed by Sattva and the result is unchanged either way.

propositions.text: The application judge erred by: (1) focusing on City's contemplation for mutual intent, (2) not requiring 'special' contemplation, (3) relying on broad wording despite contrary context.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal concluded that the application judge made three extricable errors of law, in holding that: (1) what was in the contemplation of the City was determinative of mutual intent, (2) it was not necessary to determine what was “specially” in the contemplation of the parties, and (3) it was sufficient that the broad general wording of the release covered the third party claim when the surrounding circumstances suggested otherwise.

propositions.text: These errors materially affected the result, justifying correctness review by the Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal concluded that these errors had a material effect on the result, entitling the Court of Appeal to review the decision below on a correctness standard.

propositions.text: The release's broad phrases should be read with specific Bailey Action references; correspondence did not mention Temple Action or future third party claims.
propositions.quote: It reasoned that the broad phrases in the release should be considered against the more specific references to the Bailey Action, and that the pre-contract exchange of correspondence made no reference to the Temple Action or any future third party action.

propositions.text: Words, context, and correspondence support interpreting the release as only releasing Baileys' claims in the Bailey Action.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal concluded that the words, the context, and the exchange of correspondence were all consistent with the release being interpreted as a release only of the Baileys’ claims in the Bailey Action.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal reinstated the third party notice.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal reinstated the third party notice.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found errors in the application judge's reasoning and reinstated the third party claim.

propositions.text: The City argues Blackmore Rule is obsolete; release should be interpreted by normal contractual rules; words cover all claims from accident; no factual basis to narrow scope.
propositions.quote: The City argues that the Blackmore Rule is no longer applicable and that the release should be interpreted in accordance with the normal rules of contractual interpretation. It submits that the words of the agreement plainly describe its subject matter as all claims arising from the accident, and that there is nothing in the factual matrix that could narrow this subject matter without departing from the words of the agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The City argues Blackmore is obsolete and the release covers all accident claims under normal contract interpretation.

propositions.text: Mrs. Bailey agrees Blackmore is subsumed by Sattva; whether using Blackmore or not, release bars Baileys' claims but not City's responsibility for Mr. Temple's injuries.
propositions.quote: Mrs. Bailey agrees the Blackmore Rule has been subsumed into the general principles of contractual interpretation articulated in Sattva, and submits that whether the release is interpreted using the Blackmore Rule or not, the result is the same. The release foreclosed the Baileys’ right to make any claim for injuries suffered by them arising from the accident, but the release was not intended to allocate to the Baileys the City’s responsibility for Mr. Temple’s injuries.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Bailey agrees Blackmore is subsumed by Sattva and release bars Baileys' claims but not City's liability for Mr. Temple.

propositions.text: The Court will begin analysis by outlining the contractual interpretation rule from Sattva.
propositions.quote: In order properly to consider the issues in this case, I will begin the analysis that follows with an outline of the guiding rule for the interpretation of contracts as set out by this Court in Sattva.

paragraphs.summary: The Court begins analysis by outlining Sattva's contractual interpretation rule.

propositions.text: Sattva changed contract interpretation from pure law to mixed fact and law, considering circumstances beyond ambiguity.
propositions.quote: Sattva marked a significant change in the jurisprudence. Traditionally, the interpretation of contracts was a matter of law, not mixed fact and law. This was because interpretation was seen primarily as an exercise in giving meaning to words. Circumstances were generally relevant to interpretation only where there was an ambiguity.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains Sattva changed contract interpretation to mixed fact and law, considering circumstances beyond ambiguity.

propositions.text: Blackmore Rule arose when courts avoided considering facts in contract interpretation, focusing on literal meaning.
propositions.quote: The Blackmore Rule was formulated in the traditional period to which I have just referred. In that view, courts were reluctant to have regard to the facts surrounding the formation of a contract, as an aid to its interpretation. The words of a contract were given their “black letter” meaning. This was problematic from the view of releases; the Blackmore Rule addressed this problem.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains Blackmore arose when courts avoided facts and focused on literal contract meaning, causing problems for releases.

propositions.text: Today, facts surrounding contract formation are relevant to interpretation; Blackmore Rule is no longer needed and should be abandoned.
propositions.quote: But 150 years after the Blackmore decision, things have changed. The facts surrounding the formation of a contract are relevant to its interpretation. The jurisprudential concerns that gave rise to the rule in Blackmore no longer exist. It is no longer needed. It has outlived its usefulness and should no longer be referred to.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states facts are now relevant to contract interpretation and Blackmore Rule is obsolete and should be abandoned.

propositions.text: Sattva requires reading contract as whole, giving words ordinary meaning consistent with known surrounding circumstances.
propositions.quote: This Court set out the current approach to contractual interpretation in Sattva. Sattva directs courts to “read the contract as a whole, giving the words used their ordinary and grammatical meaning, consistent with the surrounding circumstances known to the parties at the time of formation of the contract”: para. 47.

propositions.text: Meaning derives from contextual factors like purpose and relationship, but circumstances must not overwhelm contract words.
propositions.quote: This Court explained that “[t]he meaning of words is often derived from a number of contextual factors, including the purpose of the agreement and the nature of the relationship created by the agreement”, but that the surrounding circumstances “must never be allowed to overwhelm the words of that agreement”: paras. 48 and 57.

propositions.text: Courts cannot use surrounding circumstances to deviate from contract text and create a new agreement.
propositions.quote: “While the surrounding circumstances are relied upon in the interpretive process, courts cannot use them to deviate from the text such that the court effectively creates a new agreement”: para. 57.

propositions.text: Relevant circumstances are objective background facts known or reasonably known to both parties at contract formation.
propositions.quote: This Court also clarified that the relevant surrounding circumstances “consist only of objective evidence of the background facts at the time of the execution of the contract. . . , that is, knowledge that was or reasonably ought to have been within the knowledge of both parties at or before the date of contracting”: para. 58.

paragraphs.summary: The Court outlines Sattva's approach: read contract as whole, words given ordinary meaning with known circumstances, but not overriding text.

propositions.text: A release is a contract and general principles of contractual interpretation apply.
propositions.quote: A release is a contract, and these general principles of contractual interpretation apply: G. R. Hall, Canadian Contractual Interpretation Law (4th ed. 2020), at p. 286; F. D. Cass, The Law of Releases in Canada (2006), at p. 71.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule limits general words in a release to things specially contemplated by the parties at the time of release.
propositions.quote: The general words in a release are limited always to that thing or those things which were specially in the contemplation of the parties at the time when the release was given.

propositions.text: A dispute or question not arisen cannot be bound by anticipatory words of a general release.
propositions.quote: But a dispute that had not emerged, or a question which had not at all arisen, cannot be considered as bound and concluded by the anticipatory words of a general release.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a release is a contract and cites the Blackmore Rule limiting release scope to things contemplated at release time.

propositions.text: The appellant calls the principle the 'Blackmore Rule'.
propositions.quote: The appellant refers to this as the “Blackmore Rule”.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule is a special rule added to regular contractual interpretation rules.
propositions.quote: Hall describes it as a “special rule which is superadded onto the regular ones”: p. 286.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule has deep historical roots reviewed by various courts and authors.
propositions.quote: This rule has deep roots, as reviewed by Lord Bingham in Bank of Credit and Commerce International S.A. v. Ali...

propositions.text: A release cannot apply to circumstances unknown to a party at execution; overly general releases allow relief.
propositions.quote: [I]t is a principle long sanctioned in Courts of equity, that a release cannot apply, or be intended to apply to circumstances of which a party had no knowledge at the time he executed it...

paragraphs.summary: The appellant calls it the Blackmore Rule, a special rule with deep roots limiting releases to known circumstances at execution.

propositions.text: 18th and 19th century judges were less sensitive to context and reluctant to admit extrinsic evidence.
propositions.quote: Lord Hoffmann observed in Ali that judges in the 18th and 19th centuries were “less sensitive to context” and “were reluctant to admit what was called ‘extrinsic evidence’...

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule was useful under a strict 'black letter' framework excluding extrinsic evidence.
propositions.quote: While the Blackmore Rule would no doubt have had utility within that “black letter” framework, this is no longer the case.

propositions.text: Sattva directs judges to consider surrounding circumstances in contract interpretation.
propositions.quote: In Sattva, this Court directed judges to look to the surrounding circumstances known to the parties at the time of contract in interpreting the meaning of the words of a contract: para. 47.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule is overtaken by the general rule considering factual context in contract interpretation.
propositions.quote: The Blackmore Rule, which allowed courts to consider factual context when that was not the general rule, has been overtaken by a general rule that factual context is considered in interpreting contracts.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Blackmore Rule was useful under old strict rules but is now overtaken by Sattva's contextual approach.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule was adopted in Canada but interpreted narrowly and adds nothing new post-Sattva.
propositions.quote: The Blackmore Rule was adopted in Canada, but as I will explain, it was interpreted narrowly. It no longer adds anything new to the regular repertoire of contractual interpretation principles in the wake of Sattva.

propositions.text: There are two ways the Blackmore Rule was narrowly interpreted.
propositions.quote: There are two ways in which the Blackmore Rule was narrowly interpreted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Blackmore Rule was narrowly interpreted in Canada and no longer adds to contractual interpretation principles.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule does not allow consideration of parties' subjective intentions.
propositions.quote: First, the Blackmore Rule does not allow consideration of the subjective intention of the parties.

propositions.text: La Forest J.A. held 'specially in the contemplation' means surrounding circumstances, not subjective intentions.
propositions.quote: La Forest J.A. (as he then was) held in White v. Central Trust Co... that this does not refer to the subjective intention of the parties, but merely permits courts to look to the surrounding circumstances to give meaning to the words the parties used.

propositions.text: It is well-established that the Blackmore Rule excludes subjective intentions.
propositions.quote: It is well-established that the Blackmore Rule does not allow courts to consider the subjective intentions of the parties: see Hill v. Nova Scotia...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Blackmore Rule excludes subjective intentions, relying on La Forest J.A. and established case law.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule does not preclude releasing unknown claims if clear wording is used.
propositions.quote: Second, the Blackmore Rule does not preclude parties from releasing unknown claims.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal held releases can include unknown claims with clear wording in Biancaniello.
propositions.quote: In Biancaniello, the Court of Appeal for Ontario applied the Blackmore Rule and held that where sufficiently clear wording is used, releases can include claims unknown to the parties: para. 42, point 2.

propositions.text: Lord Bingham in Ali held parties may release unknown claims if language clearly shows intention.
propositions.quote: Lord Bingham reviewed... and concluded that “[a] party may . . . agree to release claims or rights of which he is unaware... if appropriate language is used to make plain that that is his intention”: para. 9.

propositions.text: Lord Nicholls agreed that general releases often intend to cover unknown claims to achieve finality.
propositions.quote: Lord Nicholls agreed, and wrote... The parties wanted to achieve finality... The mere fact that the parties were unaware... is not a reason for excluding it from the scope of the release.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Blackmore Rule allows releasing unknown claims with clear language, citing Biancaniello and Ali.

propositions.text: A release can cover unknown claims without precise particularization if wording is sufficient.
propositions.quote: A release can cover an unknown claim with sufficient language, and does not necessarily need to particularize with precision the exact claims that fall within its scope.

propositions.text: Parties bargain for finality in releases, accepting risk of unknown claims being released.
propositions.quote: In entering into a release, the parties bargain for finality... The releasor takes on the risk of relinquishing the value of the claims he or she might have had...

propositions.text: Difficulty arises in deciding what wording suffices to encompass unknown claims.
propositions.quote: Of course, difficulty can arise in deciding what wording is sufficient to encompass the unknown claim at issue in a given case.

propositions.text: Releases can encompass unknown claims; the Blackmore Rule has not been interpreted to say otherwise.
propositions.quote: However, it is clear that releases can encompass such claims, and the Blackmore Rule has not been interpreted to hold otherwise.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains releases can cover unknown claims with sufficient wording, reflecting parties' bargain for finality.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule no longer adds to or deviates from general contract interpretation principles post-Sattva.
propositions.quote: In light of the narrow manner in which the Blackmore Rule has been interpreted, and in light of Sattva... the Blackmore Rule no longer adds to or deviates from the general principles of interpretation that apply to all contracts.

propositions.text: Hall agrees the Blackmore Rule is consistent with general contract interpretation law.
propositions.quote: I agree with Hall that the Blackmore Rule “is entirely consistent with the law of contractual interpretation generally”: p. 286.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Blackmore Rule is consistent with general contract interpretation and adds nothing new post-Sattva.

propositions.text: Some Canadian appellate courts apply the Blackmore Rule similarly to ordinary contractual interpretation principles.
propositions.quote: While some Canadian appellate courts have purported to apply the Blackmore Rule, the way in which the Rule is expressed in these cases is no different from ordinary principles of contractual interpretation.

propositions.text: BC Court of Appeal in Bank of British Columbia Pension Plan applied principles resembling the Blackmore Rule consistent with Sattva.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal for British Columbia summarized the interpretive principles... resembling the Blackmore Rule, but it is applied in a way that is entirely consistent with the approach set out in Sattva.

propositions.text: The BC Court interpreted a release broadly to include rights not explicitly mentioned but within parties' contemplation.
propositions.quote: In Bank of British Columbia, the court interpreted a release... broadly to include any rights... even though his rights... were not explicitly mentioned in the release.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Canadian appellate courts apply the Blackmore Rule as ordinary contract interpretation, consistent with Sattva.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal in Biancaniello applied Blackmore Rule principles but interpreted release broadly to include unknown negligence claims.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal for Ontario... interpreted the release at issue in Biancaniello broadly... to include subsequently discovered negligence on the part of the firm.

propositions.text: Negligence unknown at contract time was within parties' contemplation as subject matter covered by release.
propositions.quote: Negligence that was unknown to the parties at the time of contract was held to be within their contemplation or mutual intention given that the claim fell within the “subject matter” covered by the release.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule's formulation and application in these cases aligns with general contractual interpretation principles.
propositions.quote: The way the Blackmore Rule is formulated and applied in both these cases reveals no inconsistency with the general principles of contractual interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Biancaniello applied the Blackmore Rule but interpreted releases broadly, consistent with general contract principles.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule can yield narrow release interpretations excluding claims arising after release signing.
propositions.quote: It is true that the application of the Blackmore Rule can yield a narrow interpretation of releases, because courts can rely on it to hold that a claim that arose after the release was signed was not in the contemplation of the parties and is therefore not covered.

propositions.text: BC Court of Appeal in Privest Properties applied Blackmore Rule narrowly to exclude later-known claims.
propositions.quote: In Privest Properties Ltd. v. Foundation Co. of Canada... the Court of Appeal for British Columbia applied the Blackmore Rule to interpret a release narrowly and hold that it did not apply to all potential future litigation.

propositions.text: This Court in Hill relied on Blackmore Rule to read release narrowly, excluding bar to compensation for equitable interest.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in Hill, this Court relied on the Blackmore Rule in reading a release narrowly and held that... the release therefore could not constitute a bar to compensation to the appellants for the taking of their equitable interest in the land.

propositions.text: The same conclusions could be reached by applying Sattva principles without Blackmore Rule.
propositions.quote: However, it seems to me that the same conclusion could have been reached in these cases by simply applying the principles set out in Sattva.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges Blackmore Rule can narrow releases but similar results follow from Sattva principles alone.

propositions.text: Whether using Blackmore Rule or not, the result is the same; application judge's reliance on it is immaterial.
propositions.quote: Therefore, as the Court of Appeal concluded in the present case, whether one approaches the matter on the basis of the Blackmore Rule or not, the result is the same, and the application judge’s reliance on the Blackmore Rule is of no moment.

propositions.text: The application judge's conclusion about parties' contemplation aligns with Sattva's mutual, objective intention language.
propositions.quote: As I read the application judge’s reasons, his conclusion about what the parties “contemplated” is synonymous with the language from Sattva about what the parties mutually, objectively intended: Sattva, at para. 57.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the application judge's reliance on the Blackmore Rule immaterial as his conclusion aligns with Sattva.

propositions.text: The Blackmore Rule and related jurisprudence should no longer be referred to as their function is subsumed by Sattva's approach.
propositions.quote: The Blackmore Rule and the jurisprudence pursuant to it should no longer be referred to, as the function that it had served has been subsumed entirely by the approach set out in Sattva.

propositions.text: Lord Nicholls in Ali stated no special rules of interpretation apply to general releases; general contract principles apply.
propositions.quote: As Lord Nicholls put it in Ali, at para. 26: . . . there is no room today for the application of any special “rules” of interpretation in the case of general releases...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Blackmore Rule is subsumed by Sattva and cites Lord Nicholls that no special rules apply to releases.

propositions.text: Contract interpretation has evolved to a practical, common-sense approach not dominated by technical rules.
propositions.quote: This uniform understanding of the principles of contractual interpretation is consistent with this Court’s guidance in Sattva that “the interpretation of contracts has evolved towards a practical, common-sense approach not dominated by technical rules of construction”: para. 47.

propositions.text: No special rule of contractual interpretation applies only to releases.
propositions.quote: There is no special rule of contractual interpretation that applies only to releases.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms contract interpretation is practical and common-sense, with no special rule for releases.

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation requires giving words ordinary meaning consistent with surrounding circumstances known at contract formation.
propositions.quote: Contractual interpretation requires courts to give the words of a contract their ordinary and grammatical meaning, in a way that is consistent with the surrounding circumstances known to the parties at the time of contract formation: Sattva, at paras. 47-48.

propositions.text: Sometimes tension arises between ordinary meaning and surrounding circumstances, requiring courts to decide which prevails.
propositions.quote: Sometimes the ordinary meaning of the words and the surrounding circumstances come into tension, and courts must decide whether to rely on the surrounding circumstances to refine the meaning of the words, or whether doing so would impermissibly overwhelm the words of the agreements, in which case the words must override: para. 57.

propositions.text: This tension may arise more often when interpreting releases, for two reasons.
propositions.quote: This tension may more often arise when interpreting releases, for two reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains contract interpretation balances words and context, with tension more common in releases for two reasons.

propositions.text: Releases are often expressed in the broadest possible words.
propositions.quote: First, as Cass observes, “A distinctive feature of releases is that they are often expressed in the broadest possible words”: p. 83 (footnote omitted).

propositions.text: A general release literally could prevent suing forever, but may not reflect parties' objective intention.
propositions.quote: A general release, if interpreted literally, could prevent the releasor from suing the releasee for any reason, forever. While such a release may not be enforceable for other reasons... the circumstances may also often indicate that such extreme consequences are not what the parties objectively intended.

propositions.text: BC Court of Appeal said broad releases must be considered in context of the dispute, limiting their breadth.
propositions.quote: As the Court of Appeal for British Columbia put it in Strata Plan BCS 327, “While releases signed in the course of a settlement of a dispute are often worded in a broad and general fashion... they must be considered in the context of the dispute”: para. 26.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes releases are often broadly worded but context limits their scope, as BC Court of Appeal held.

propositions.text: Parties to releases often try to account for unknown risks, creating imprecision and potential disagreement.
propositions.quote: Second, parties to a release are often trying to account for risks that at the time of contract are unknown. There is an imprecision inherent in this task; this can give rise to disagreement as to what was intended.

propositions.text: Lord Nicholls in Ali explained parties want to 'wipe the slate clean' but unknown claims may arise later.
propositions.quote: As Lord Nicholls wrote in Ali, parties settling a dispute want “to wipe the slate clean”, but it is not unusual for a claim to come to light whose existence was not known or suspected by either party.

propositions.text: The emergence of unknown claims raises whether the release's context limits its broad wording.
propositions.quote: The emergence of such an unsuspected claim gives rise to the question of “whether the context in which the general release was given is apt to cut down the apparently all-embracing scope of the words of the release”: para. 23.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains parties accept unknown risks in releases, raising issues whether context limits broad wording.

propositions.text: Releases often cause tension between broad wording and parties' objective intention more than other contracts.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, releases may tend to lead to dissonance between the words of the agreement on their face and what the parties seem to have objectively intended based on the surrounding circumstances, with greater regularity than other types of contracts: see Cass, at p. 89.

propositions.text: Courts may interpret releases narrowly due to broad wording conflicting with circumstances, not due to special rules.
propositions.quote: courts can be persuaded to interpret releases narrowly more so than other types of contracts, not because there is any special rule of interpretation that applies to releases, but simply because the broad wording of releases can conflict with the circumstances...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds releases often cause tension leading courts to interpret them narrowly due to broad wording, not special rules.

propositions.text: In Ali, House of Lords agreed releases can include unknown claims but courts are cautious absent clear language.
propositions.quote: In Ali, the House of Lords unanimously agreed that it is possible for a release to include claims of which the parties were not aware... but “in the absence of clear language, the court will be very slow to infer that a party intended to surrender rights and claims of which he was unaware...”: para. 10.

propositions.text: The authorities provide a cautionary principle, not a rule of law, guiding courts' approach to unknown claims in releases.
propositions.quote: He explained that the authorities provide “not a rule of law but a cautionary principle which should inform the approach of the court”: para. 17.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Ali that releases can include unknown claims but courts apply a cautionary principle absent clear language.

propositions.text: Lord Nicholls warned the approach to unknown claims in releases should not be pressed too far; context matters.
propositions.quote: Lord Nicholls warned that while a release can include unknown claims, this approach “should not be pressed too far” as “the circumstances in which the release was given may suggest... that the release should apply only to claims... relating to a particular subject matter”: para. 28.

propositions.text: Example: a mutual general release on partnership accounts may not cover unrelated claims like property damage.
propositions.quote: Lord Nicholls gave the example of a mutual general release on a settlement of final partnership accounts... such a release may be properly confined to claims arising out of the partnership, and could not be taken to preclude a claim... that tree roots... had damaged... a neighbouring partner’s house.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Lord Nicholls that releases including unknown claims should be limited by context and subject matter.

propositions.text: House of Lords unanimously held unknown claims can be released but did not specify sufficient language
propositions.quote: While the House of Lords was unanimous that it is possible to release unknown claims, they did not make clear what language would be sufficient.

propositions.text: Lord Hoffmann dissented against excessive verbiage in release language
propositions.quote: As Lord Hoffmann pointed out in dissent, the answer is not to encourage “grosser excesses of verbiage”: para. 38.

propositions.text: Cass agrees and suggests release wording clarify coverage of unknown claims and subject matter
propositions.quote: Cass agrees, and writes, at p. 99: “One hopes that it is not to be expected that the release will catalogue with specificity all possible claims . . . .” Cass suggests that the drafter of a release might consider wording that makes clear whether the release will cover unknown claims and whether the claims must be related to a particular area or subject matter.

propositions.text: Releases narrowed by time or subject matter less likely to conflict with parties' objective intent
propositions.quote: I would add that releases that are narrowed to a particular time frame or subject matter are less likely to give rise to tension between the words and what the surrounding circumstances indicate the parties objectively intended.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds House of Lords agreed unknown claims can be released but language sufficiency unclear; Cass suggests clear wording; court adds narrowing releases reduces tension with intent.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal broadly interpreted release to include unknown claims in Biancaniello
propositions.quote: In that case, the Court of Appeal for Ontario applied the principles from Ali to interpret a release broadly to include unknown claims.

propositions.text: Release barred all claims from services to a certain date including claims in fee dispute action
propositions.quote: The release barred “any and all claims arising from any and all services” provided by the firm to its client through to a certain date, and “without limiting the generality of the foregoing” any and all claims, counterclaims or defences that could have been pleaded in the fee dispute action: para. 6 (emphasis deleted).

propositions.text: Feldman J.A. found release included claims from subsequently discovered negligence without further specification
propositions.quote: Feldman J.A., writing for the court, interpreted the release broadly to include claims arising from the firm’s subsequently discovered negligence. She noted that the release was limited to claims that existed up to a certain date, and to claims arising from the services provided by the accountants to their client. There was no need to further specify the types of claims that were included.

propositions.text: No need to list claim types; unknown claims included unless specifically excluded
propositions.quote: There is no need, for example, to say ‘including tort claims, negligence claims, breach of contract claims, cost claims’, etc. They are all included unless specifically excluded. The same analysis applies to unknown claims. . . . Had it said ‘including known and unknown claims’, that would just have been another way of saying that the release includes all claims.”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds Ontario Court of Appeal broadly interpreted release in Biancaniello to include unknown claims without listing types.

propositions.text: Distinction between claims based on known and unknown facts relevant to release interpretation
propositions.quote: Distinctions can be drawn between claims based on facts known to both parties (as in this case) and claims based on facts that were not known to both parties (as in Biancaniello). Such distinctions may be relevant when interpreting a release and assessing whether the claim at issue is the kind of claim the parties mutually intended to release.

propositions.text: Ultimate question is whether claim is type the release is directed to, depending on wording and circumstances
propositions.quote: The ultimate question is whether the claim is of the type of claim to which the release is directed. This will depend on the wording and surrounding circumstances of the release in each case.

propositions.text: Lord Bingham’s caution in Ali is an observation, not a rule of interpretation
propositions.quote: Lord Bingham’s cautionary principle from Ali should be understood not as a rule of interpretation, but rather an observation as to the issues that releases will tend to give rise to given their subject matter.

propositions.text: Judicial narrowing of broad wording is contextual, ordinary contract interpretation rules apply
propositions.quote: Any judicial tendency to narrow the meaning given to broad wording is not the function of any special rule, but rather a function of the context in which releases are given. Thus, the ordinary rules for contract interpretation set out in Sattva apply to releases as they do to other contracts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds distinctions between known and unknown claims matter; interpretation depends on wording and context; Ali’s caution is observational; Sattva rules apply.

propositions.text: Contract interpretation is fact-specific mixed question of fact and law unless extricable question of law
propositions.quote: In Sattva, this Court also explained that contractual interpretation is a fact specific exercise, and should be treated as a mixed question of fact and law for the purpose of appellate review, unless there is an “extricable question of law”.

propositions.text: Extricable questions include incorrect principle application, failure to consider legal test element or relevant factor
propositions.quote: Extricable questions of law in the context of contractual interpretation include “the application of an incorrect principle, the failure to consider a required element of a legal test, or the failure to consider a relevant factor”: Sattva, at para. 53, quoting King v. Operating Engineers Training Institute of Manitoba Inc., 2011 MBCA 80, 270 Man. R. (2d) 63, at para. 21.

propositions.text: Questions of law extraction in contract interpretation are uncommon
propositions.quote: The circumstances in which a question of law can be extracted will be uncommon.

propositions.text: Whether something was or should have been within parties’ common knowledge is a question of fact
propositions.quote: Whether something was or should have been within the common knowledge of the parties at the time the contract was entered into is a question of fact: Sattva, at paras. 49-55 and 58.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Sattva holds contract interpretation is fact-specific mixed question, extricable law questions are rare, and common knowledge is factual.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found three extricable errors of law by application judge
propositions.quote: In the present case, the Court of Appeal held that the application judge made three errors on extricable questions of law, at paras. 50-52: Firstly, what was in the contemplation of the City in drafting the Release is not determinative of mutual intent. Secondly, it was in fact necessary to determine what was “specifically” contemplated by both parties. Thirdly, it was not sufficient that the broad general wording of the Release potentially covered a subsequent third party action for contribution if the surrounding circumstances suggested otherwise.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports Court of Appeal found three extricable legal errors by application judge.

propositions.text: Disagrees that application judge erred on extricable questions of law
propositions.quote: I disagree that any of these constitutes an error warranting appellate intervention.

propositions.text: Application judge considered City's contemplation but did not treat it as determinative of mutual intent
propositions.quote: The application judge did consider what was objectively contemplated or intended by the City, but it is clear that he did not consider this to be determinative of mutual intent.

propositions.text: Application judge explicitly considered both parties' contemplation and concluded release barred all claims relating to accident
propositions.quote: The application judge explicitly considers what was in the contemplation of both parties beginning at para. 29. He explains that the Baileys could have negotiated the terms of the release, but that they chose not to, and he concludes that “what was in the contemplation of the parties was that Mrs. Bailey could no longer bring any claim or demand whatsoever against the City relating to the Accident”: para. 43; see also paras. 41-42 and 44.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal mischaracterized application judge's approach
propositions.quote: With respect, the Court of Appeal mischaracterized what the application judge did.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Court of Appeal, finds application judge considered contemplation properly and was mischaracterized.

propositions.text: Second and third Court of Appeal points are not extricable questions of law
propositions.quote: The second and third points are not extricable questions of law.

propositions.text: Sattva holds common knowledge questions are factual
propositions.quote: This Court held in Sattva that whether something was or reasonably should have been within the common knowledge of both parties at the time a contract was entered into is a question of fact.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal wrongly treated surrounding circumstances interpretation as extricable question of law
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal treated the question of how the surrounding circumstances inform the words of a contract as an “extricable question of law”.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal substituted its factual conclusions improperly
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal simply disagreed with the application judge’s interpretation of the surrounding circumstances, characterized it as a question of law, and then substituted its own factual conclusions.

propositions.text: This approach conflicts with Sattva's deferential appellate review of contract interpretation
propositions.quote: This does not accord with Sattva.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Court of Appeal erred by treating factual surrounding circumstances as extricable law and substituting findings, conflicting with Sattva.

propositions.text: Application judge considered surrounding circumstances and mutual intention
propositions.quote: The application judge considered the surrounding circumstances, and he made a finding about what was in the contemplation or mutual intention of both parties: paras. 23 and 43.

propositions.text: Application judge found parties contemplated all claims relating to accident including third party claim
propositions.quote: he made a finding about what was in the contemplation or mutual intention of both parties: paras. 23 and 43. The application judge went on to conclude that it was not “necessary that the parties be specifically contemplating a particular type of claim. Instead . . . it is sufficient [that] the parties were contemplating any and all types of claims relating to a particular event such as the Accident”: para. 44.

propositions.text: This fact-specific application of contract principles was owed deference
propositions.quote: This holding is a fact-specific application of the principles of contractual interpretation, and it was owed deference.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds application judge considered circumstances and found parties contemplated all accident claims, a fact-specific finding owed deference.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal criticized application judge for not considering Baileys' knowledge of Temple action
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal criticizes the application judge for failing to consider “the Baileys’ continuing knowledge of the Temple action and whether it could realistically be said to continue to have been in their contemplation when the Release was signed”

propositions.text: This criticism is not an error because subjective knowledge is irrelevant under objective contract theory
propositions.quote: But this is not an error either. Mrs. Bailey’s subjective knowledge of the Temple Action, or lack thereof, is irrelevant under an objective theory of contract law, because unless that knowledge was communicated to the City, it is not a “surrounding circumstance” within the “common knowledge” of the parties: Sattva, at para. 58.

propositions.text: Private knowledge of one party does not affect contract meaning under objective theory
propositions.quote: What is privately in the mind of one party could not affect how that party’s conduct would appear to a reasonable observer in the position of the other: see Owners, Strata Plan LMS 3905 v. Crystal Square Parking Corp., 2020 SCC SCC 29, [2020] 3 S.C.R. XXX, at para. 33.

propositions.text: No comment on remedy for sharp practice of nondisclosure but private knowledge irrelevant to interpretation
propositions.quote: I make no comment on the possibility that the law may provide a remedy for the sharp practice of a releasee who intentionally does not disclose the existence of a claim to the releasor, as noted by Lord Nicholls in Ali, at paras. 32-33, and by Lord Hoffmann, at paras. 67-71. However, the fact that Mrs. Bailey, the releasor, may have had private knowledge of a claim is irrelevant in interpreting the release to determine whether or not she accidentally released that claim.

propositions.text: Lord Hoffmann in Ali: contract meaning not affected by facts known to one party but not reasonably available to other
propositions.quote: As Lord Hoffmann observed in Ali, at para. 49: “It would be contrary to basic principles of construction for the meaning of a document to be affected by facts which were known to one party but not reasonably available to the other.”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Court of Appeal's criticism is not error; subjective knowledge irrelevant under objective contract law; private knowledge does not affect meaning.

propositions.text: Application judge did not rely on Mrs. Bailey’s subjective knowledge in assessing mutual intent
propositions.quote: The application judge did not rely on Mrs. Bailey’s subjective knowledge of the Temple Action in assessing the parties’ mutual intent.

propositions.text: Application judge found Mrs. Bailey was aware or ought to be aware of Temple Action but this did not form part of contemplation analysis
propositions.quote: He did find it “noteworthy” that Mrs. Bailey was aware or ought to have been aware of the Temple Action when she signed the release, having already been served with the statement of claim, but this observation did not form part of his analysis of “what was in the contemplation of the parties”: para. 29.

propositions.text: Application judge avoided error made by Court of Appeal despite lack of clarity
propositions.quote: While not a model of clarity, he therefore avoided falling into the same error as the Court of Appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds application judge did not rely on subjective knowledge in intent assessment and avoided Court of Appeal's error.

propositions.text: No reviewable error in application judge’s conclusion that release wording includes Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim
propositions.quote: I see no reviewable error in the application judge’s conclusion that the wording of the release encompasses Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim.

propositions.text: Release wording is broad and includes all claims relating to accident including third party claims
propositions.quote: The release includes “all actions, suits, causes of action . . . foreseen or unforeseen . . . and claims of any kind or nature whatsoever arising out of or relating to the accident which occurred on or about March 3, 2009”. This wording encompasses Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim, arising out of Mr. Temple’s damages from the accident.

propositions.text: If wording insufficient, no wording short of listing every claim type would suffice
propositions.quote: If this wording is held to be insufficient to include a claim arising out of the accident, it is hard to imagine what wording would be sufficient, aside from listing every type of claim imaginable one by one (third party claims, cross claims, counter claims, subrogated claims, claims in equity and common law, statutory claims, etc.).

propositions.text: No principled reason to require parties to particularize release scope in detail
propositions.quote: There is no principled reason to require parties to particularize the scope of the release in this fashion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in application judge's broad interpretation of release including third party claims and no need for detailed listing.

propositions.text: Next release clause affirms broad interpretation by referencing claims raised or raisable in Bailey Action
propositions.quote: The next clause of the release affirms this broad interpretation. The contract does specifically reference “claims raised or which could have been raised in the [Bailey Action]”, but it references these claims in the context of specifying that the foregoing generality of the release is not limited to them.

propositions.text: This indicates the generality of release is broader than claims in Bailey Action
propositions.quote: This indicates that the “foregoing” is more general than claims that were or could have been raised in the Bailey Action.

propositions.text: Otherwise preceding portion would be redundant
propositions.quote: Otherwise the portion of the release that precedes “without limiting the generality of the foregoing” would be redundant.

propositions.text: Application judge made these points and no palpable error found
propositions.quote: The application judge makes these points at paras. 21-22. There is no palpable and overriding error in his reading.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds release clause confirms broad scope beyond Bailey Action claims; application judge's reading is correct.

propositions.text: No palpable error in application judge’s finding that surrounding circumstances support broad reading
propositions.quote: There is also no palpable and overriding error in the application judge’s finding that the surrounding circumstances are consistent with this reading.

propositions.text: Both parties knew Mrs. Bailey struck City employee and knew each other knew
propositions.quote: Both the City and the Baileys were aware that Mrs. Bailey had struck a City employee with her car, and both were aware that the other knew.

propositions.text: Pleadings show knowledge of accident and potential claims
propositions.quote: This is obvious from the pleadings exchanged by the City and the Baileys in the Bailey Action.

propositions.text: Both parties knew or ought to know City employee may have claim against Mrs. Bailey or City
propositions.quote: Both the City and Mrs. Bailey therefore knew, or ought to have known on an objective basis, that the City employee who had been hit may have an outstanding claim against Mrs. Bailey, or the City, or both,

propositions.text: Such claim could put parties in adverse positions and incentivize blame shifting
propositions.quote: and that such a claim could put the City and Mrs. Bailey in an adverse position to one another, where it would be to both of their advantages to blame the damage on the other.

propositions.text: This factual matrix supports interpreting release as including third party claim
propositions.quote: This aspect of the factual matrix weighs in favour of interpreting the words of the release as including Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim in the Temple Action.

propositions.text: Application judge explains this at paras. 27-28
propositions.quote: The application judge explains this at paras. 27-28 of his reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in application judge's finding that circumstances support broad release including third party claim.

propositions.text: Application judge concluded parties contemplated all claim types relating to accident
propositions.quote: The application judge concluded that “it is sufficient [that] the parties were contemplating any and all types of claims relating to a particular event such as the Accident”.

propositions.text: Parties narrowed release to claims from particular event, reducing tension between words and circumstances
propositions.quote: because the parties narrowed the subject matter of the release to claims arising out of a particular event, the application judge found no tension between the words and the surrounding circumstances.

propositions.text: As in Biancaniello, circumscribed release and circumstances support plain reading
propositions.quote: As in Biancaniello, the release was circumscribed, and nothing in the surrounding circumstances indicated to the application judge that the words of the release should be interpreted to depart from what on a plain reading they would mean.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds application judge concluded parties contemplated all accident claims; narrowing release reduces tension; Biancaniello supports plain reading.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal noted $7,500 settlement quantum not inconsistent with releasing only Baileys’ claims
propositions.quote: In its own interpretation of the release, the Court of Appeal observed that the quantum of “only $7,500” was “not inconsistent” with the conclusion that the parties intended to release only the Baileys’ claims: paras. 63-64.

propositions.text: $7,500 settlement quantum also not inconsistent with application judge’s interpretation
propositions.quote: This may be true, but the settlement quantum of $7,500 is also not inconsistent with the application judge’s interpretation,

propositions.text: No evidence of City’s liability to compare settlement quantum
propositions.quote: and in any case, there is no evidence in the record of the City’s liability against which to compare the settlement quantum.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Court of Appeal's settlement quantum observation is true but also consistent with application judge; no liability evidence to compare.

propositions.text: Application judge considered pre-contract negotiations in mutual intent conclusion
propositions.quote: The application judge also considered the pre-contract negotiations in reaching his conclusion that the parties mutually intended to release Mrs. Bailey’s claim: paras. 30-38.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal also considered negotiations but reached different conclusion
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal did too, but reached a different conclusion: paras. 67-68.

propositions.text: Neither party argued anything wrong with courts considering negotiations
propositions.quote: Neither party argued that there was anything wrong with this approach by the courts below.

propositions.text: Traditional rule excludes negotiation evidence in contract interpretation
propositions.quote: there is a longstanding, traditional rule that evidence of negotiations is inadmissible when interpreting a contract: see Resolute FP Canada Inc. v. Ontario (Attorney General), 2019 SCC 60, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 394, at para. 100, per Côté and Brown JJ., in dissent; Chartbrook Ltd. v. Persimmon Homes Ltd., [2009] UKHL 38, [2009] 1 A.C. 1101; Hall, at pp. 423-32; A. Swan, J. Adamski and A. Y. Na, Canadian Contract Law (4th ed. 2018), at pp. 745-48; K. Lewison, The Interpretation of Contracts (7th ed. 2020), at pp. 117-31; J. D. McCamus, The Law of Contracts (3rd ed. 2020), at pp. 809-13.

propositions.text: Justices Côté and Brown note tension between negotiation exclusion and Sattva surrounding circumstances approach
propositions.quote: Justices Côté and Brown observed in Resolute that this rule “sits uneasily” next to the approach from Sattva that directs courts to consider the surrounding circumstances in interpreting a contract: para. 100.

propositions.text: Hall and Canadian Contract Law authors emphasize difficulty distinguishing surrounding circumstances and negotiations
propositions.quote: Hall and the authors of Canadian Contract Law both emphasize the difficulty in drawing a principled distinction between the circumstances surrounding contract formation and negotiations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds both courts considered negotiations; traditional rule excludes negotiation evidence but tension exists with Sattva approach.

propositions.text: Leaves question of negotiation admissibility for future case
propositions.quote: I leave for another day the question of whether, and if so, in what circumstances, negotiations will be admissible in interpreting a contract.

propositions.text: Issue needs full argument and necessity to decide appeal
propositions.quote: That issue needs to await a case where it has been fully argued and is necessary in order to decide the appeal.

propositions.text: Application judge did not consider negotiations determinative here
propositions.quote: In this case, the application judge did not consider the negotiations to be determinative in interpreting the contract one way or the other: see paras. 37-38 and 41.

paragraphs.summary: The court defers deciding negotiation admissibility issue; application judge did not find negotiations determinative here.

propositions.text: No reviewable error in application judge’s conclusion that release includes Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim
propositions.quote: To conclude, there is no reviewable error in the application judge’s conclusion that the release includes Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim.

propositions.text: Claim falls within plain meaning of release words and surrounding circumstances confirm objective knowledge
propositions.quote: The claim comes within the plain meaning of the words of the release, the surrounding circumstances confirm that the parties had objective knowledge of all the facts underlying Mrs. Bailey’s third party claim when they executed the release,

propositions.text: Like Biancaniello, parties limited release scope to claims from particular event
propositions.quote: and like Biancaniello, the parties limited the scope of the release to claims arising out of a particular event.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes no error in application judge's finding that release includes third party claim, confirmed by circumstances and event limitation.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed, Court of Appeal order set aside, application judge’s order reinstated
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed, the Court of Appeal’s order is set aside and the order of the application judge is reinstated.

propositions.text: Appellant awarded costs throughout
propositions.quote: The appellant will have its costs throughout. Appeal allowed with costs throughout.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent named
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant: Stewart McKelvey, St. John’s. Solicitors for the respondent: McInnes Cooper, St. John’s.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows appeal, sets aside Court of Appeal order, reinstates application judge’s order, and awards costs to appellant.
